rounds.text: Chavda Infra Ltd demonstrates robust long-term top-line expansion, backed by a compounded sales growth of 29% over 5 years, 26% over 3 years, and 23% over the trailing twelve months [E14, E15, E16]. This consistent multi-year sales uptrend is matched by historical profitability gains, highlighted by a 30% compounded profit growth over 5 years and an operating margin that expanded to 18% in Mar 2026 from 17% three years earlier [E17, E25]. Furthermore, the business is actively deleveraging, with borrowings reduced to Rs 139 Cr in Mar 2026 down from Rs 162 Cr a year prior [E34]. Valuation metrics indicate mispricing relative to intrinsic worth, as a discounted cash flow analysis places intrinsic value at Rs 106 per share, offering a substantial margin of safety of 33.8% against the current market price of Rs 70.3 [E40, E41]. Reinforcing this valuation buffer, a reverse DCF model reveals that today's price implies only 12.3% earnings growth, which sits comfortably below the 18.0% growth assumed in the base case [E42]. Conceded: [E19], [E26], [E29], [E30], [E31], [E55], [E56].

The fundamental reality of Chavda Infra Ltd is a severe breakdown in cash generation paired with collapsing short-term profitability, despite rich valuation multiples running above sector benchmarks [E6, E7, E11, E29, E30]. Operating cash flow turned aggressively negative to Rs -8 Cr alongside free cash flow of Rs -30 Cr in March 2026, meaning the company converts a mere 3% of its operating profit into actual cash [E29, E30, E31, E32]. This liquidity squeeze is exacerbated by bloated working capital requirements, as debtor days stretched from 101 to 134 days and total working capital days blew out from 101 to 162 days [E55, E56]. Meanwhile, earnings momentum has deteriorated sharply, highlighted by a -18% trailing twelve-month profit growth rate, a steep 14% quarterly operating margin in June 2026 down seven percentage points year-over-year, and a dismal rules-based screen score of 30 out of 100 pointing to a sell rating [E19, E26, E57]. Insiders and institutional participants are actively abandoning the stock, with promoter holding plunging by nearly 18 percentage points from 73.00% to 55.12% and foreign institutional ownership completely wiped out to 0.00% [E36, E37]. Market sentiment matches this fundamental rot, as evidenced by a relative-strength rating of 0 against the Nifty 500, a twelve-month price return of -38.5%, and high annualized volatility of 60.8% [E46, E47, E49]. Conceded: [E14, E15, E16, E17, E40, E41, E42] long-term multi-year sales and profit growth figures along with discounted cash flow models suggest some intrinsic value cushion, but these historical metrics offer little comfort against ongoing operational bleeding and shareholder exits.

The bear’s focus on short-term cash flow ignores the company’s demonstrated ability to scale, as evidenced by consistent multi-year compounded sales growth of 29% over five years and 23% over the trailing twelve months [E14, E16]. While the bear highlights recent cash flow volatility, it overlooks that the company has successfully reduced its total borrowings from Rs 162 Cr to Rs 139 Cr in the same period, indicating a strategic shift toward deleveraging [E34]. Conceded: [E29, E30, E31, E32] the company is currently experiencing negative operating and free cash flow. The bear characterizes the valuation as "rich," yet this ignores the intrinsic value of Rs 106 per share, which provides a significant 33.8% margin of safety against the current market price [E40, E41]. Furthermore, the bear’s claim of "fundamental rot" is contradicted by the company’s ability to maintain an ROCE of 11.87%, which remains competitive against the sector benchmark of 11.76% [E10]. Conceded: [E36, E37] promoter holdings and foreign institutional ownership have declined. Finally, the bear’s reliance on a 30/100 screen score ignores the positive signal of a golden cross, where the 50-day moving average sits above the 200-day moving average, suggesting a potential shift in technical momentum [E57, E60].
